The election is scheduled for November 3, 2026, the same day as this search. Note that the Emerson figures appear in two different sources with different dates and sample sizes, so the timing of individual polls may be inconsistent across outlets.

Early voting for the November 3, 2026 Texas general election has ended, and the totals exceed the 2018 midterm record, though sources differ slightly on the exact count.

- **Headline figure:** Texas Tribune reports more than 7.7 million Texans voted early in the 2026 midterm election, according to preliminary data from the secretary of state's office as of Sunday morning. This puts turnout at 40.5%, surpassing the modern-day high-water mark for a midterm election set in 2018.
- **Other tallies:** Texpolls puts it at 7,711,768 Texans have voted early, 40.5% of 19,041,684 registered voters through October 30. TheOElections shows 7,744,549 Texans have voted as of Oct 30, 2026: 7,463,553 early in person and 280,996 by mail. TransparencyUSA lists 7,710,526 votes cast and a 40.1% turnout rate, using 19,228,703 registered voters as the denominator.
- **Context:** Rice University political scientist Mark Jones said "We're not going to hit presidential levels, but this is definitely high turnout". One forecast from earlier in the period suggested as many as 10 million Texans may turn out to vote, which would put 2026's final turnout in the neighborhood of 2018's 53%.

Bottom line: roughly 7.7 million early votes (about 40% of registered voters), with final turnout still pending Election Day ballots. The small differences between sources likely reflect different data cutoffs and voter-roll denominators.

The legislature passed a bill, but the most recent source I found says the governor did not sign it. Instead she issued an executive order.

- **The bill:** New York's legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act (S10642/A11560) on June 4, 2026. Lawmakers approved a one-year pause on state permits for new large data centers, defined as those with peak demand of 20 megawatts or more. The bill cleared the Senate 44–16 and the Assembly 102-39.
- **Governor's action:** A law firm alert says that on July 14, 2026, Governor Kathy Hochul signed the narrower Executive Order No. 62 rather than the bill. That order applies a one-year moratorium to data centers expected to draw more than 50 MW, a higher threshold than the legislature's 20 MW. Other sources from June still describe the bill as awaiting her decision, so the sources conflict on timing. I did not confirm the order's status in any later source.
- **Other states:** Maine's legislature passed LD 307, a moratorium on data centers above 20 MW, but it was vetoed by the governor of Maine, Janet Mills. Other states have introduced bills, with one tracker listing proposals in Maryland, New Hampshire, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, and Wisconsin.
- **Scale:** One law firm reports that more than 300 data center-related bills have been filed across more than 30 states in 2026, and at least 12 states have considered moratorium legislation.

I ran one search, so I did not check for developments after the July sources, such as whether the executive order remains in effect or whether any other state has passed a statewide pause.

The August 2026 Census figure for private data center construction is about **$84.95 billion** at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, 7.5 percent above July and 73.2 percent above August 2025. Census revised July to $79 billion from $75.2 billion. Sources describe the figure as a record for the series. The $84.95 billion number excludes "racks or servers in data centers", and power plants and transmission lines fall under a separate category.

Total U.S. construction in August was $2,203.1 billion at an annual rate, 0.9 percent above July and 1.7 percent below a year earlier. ABC reported that nonresidential construction spending rose 0.7% in August to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $1.309 trillion.

Two caveats:
- A later release has superseded August. Census's September report, published November 2, put private data center construction at a record $96.5 billion annual rate, up 90.3% from a year earlier. September figures are preliminary.
- One earlier figure is wrong. The $28.5 billion figure that circulated in earlier coverage does not match the Census data.

Here's what the search turned up. Most of it comes from coverage of the July 27, 2026 Senate Finance hearing, and the sources are not fully consistent on the numbers.

- **Cost:** The Comptroller projects the exemption will cost about $3.3 billion in the 2028–29 biennium, according to the Senate Finance Committee. That figure counts only state sales tax and excludes local property-tax abatements and infrastructure costs (it does not include local property-tax abatements or the public cost of expanding electricity and water infrastructure). An earlier Comptroller estimate was $3.2 billion over two years, and the Comptroller's chief revenue estimator has said the cost will likely rise (as data center developers rush to establish themselves in Texas, that cost will likely be higher).
- **Oversight:** Comptroller officials said data centers initially self-certify their eligibility. Per KUT, only about 20 have been audited or are currently under audit out of 138 certified.
- **Repeal push:** Sen. Brandon Creighton's successor-era chair, Sen. Paul Huffman, reportedly reiterated an earlier commitment to file legislation to either reform the tax exemption or repeal it altogether during the next legislative session. Other senators were skeptical of the exemption as written, but it was unclear if they would be willing to repeal the tax exemption entirely. Sen. Chuy Hinojosa questioned whether that level of foregone revenue is sustainable.
- **Abbott:** Abbott's position is less clear from these results. KUT reports that Abbott has called for limits on some future data center development, particularly in rural areas. One Community Impact excerpt says a "he" who was seeking reelection would work with the legislature to repeal the exemption, but the excerpt doesn't clearly name the speaker, so I wouldn't rely on it without checking.
- **Industry response:** The Data Center Coalition argues that a complete repeal of the sales tax exemption risks ending Texas' rising status as the top market for data center construction.

The sources don't confirm any repeal or reform bill has been filed for the 2027 session. Several also note that the Comptroller's next exemption study is not due until later in the year.

Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee, has made data centers a central campaign issue against Gov. Greg Abbott. Her core demand is that Abbott pause new data centers until the Legislature writes rules. She has said that if elected she would issue a moratorium on new data centers and approvals until laws protect Texans. She also wants the tax breaks ended. She requested a special session for the Texas legislature to end the tax breaks.

Abbott has moved toward restrictions. He called for sweeping regulations on data centers to be passed by the legislature in the 2027 session. He is also calling on lawmakers to repeal sales tax exemptions for data centers. In August he announced a moratorium on the approval of data centers until an audit regarding data centers' connection to the state's electric grid is conducted. Hinojosa calls his pause "in name only."

The tax break is central to the dispute. Hinojosa blames Abbott for signing House Bill 2712 in 2015, which created a 20-year sales and use tax exemption for large data center projects. Abbott's campaign counters that Hinojosa has criticized Hinojosa's own voting record on data centers during her time as a State Representative. The Daily Signal reports that she has a record of voting in favor of tax incentives for data centers during her time in the Texas House.

Public opinion favors tighter rules. One poll found 65% of likely voters supporting state legislation to regulate the impact of new data centers on infrastructure. The race has also tightened: a new poll shows the race has tightened.
